# P3 - Front-run-only or operator-delay dependency

## Intent

The attack only works if the attacker wins a race or if the operator fails to act. Front-running and delay dependencies are excluded by most programs, because the finding describes a competition rather than a bug. A bare mention of front-running is not that finding.

## Detection signals

Weak signals (front-run, mempool, sandwich, race against) hold the report. Strong signals escalate to a hard fail: front-run-only, depends entirely on ordering, before the operator calls, operator delay. An unprivileged yield theft that mentions front-running is suppressed, not held and not killed.

Patterns are case-insensitive regular expressions matched against the full text of the
draft finding, subject to the engine rules below.

**Fires when at least one of these matches:**

```text
  front[- ]?run
  mempool
  race (condition )?against
  sandwich
```

**Escalates.** A match on any of these strong forms raises the rule to `hard`, because these are the forms that name the
problem rather than hedge around it:

```text
  front[- ]?run[- ]?only
  only (by |via |through )?(a |the )?(front[- ]?run|mempool|ordering)
  depends (only |entirely |solely ) on (a |the )?(front[- ]?run|ordering|mempool)
  before the operator (calls|updates|acts)
  operator (delay|fails to act|failing to act)
```

## Escape hatches

Two kinds of suppression, plus a document-level one. Atomicity - an atomic single-transaction path, a flash loan, or "same transaction" - removes the race. A missing slippage or deadline check is a code defect that a sandwich merely exploits, and programs pay it, so it suppresses the rule too. An unprivileged caller stealing or extracting yield suppresses the rule even when front-running is also mentioned.

**Suppressed when any of these matches anywhere in the finding:**

```text
  atomic(ally)? (in )?(one|a single) transaction
  flash ?loan
  same transaction
  slippage
  min(imum)?[ _-]?(amount)?[ _-]?out
  amount_?out_?min
  \bdeadline\b
```

**Suppressed from any sentence** when one of these matches, even if `none_of` is sentence-scoped. The match is still negation-aware:

```text
  unprivileged (user|caller|attacker|address|account)[^.]{0,180}(steal|stole|stolen|drain|drains|drained|extract|extracts|extracted|profit|profits|profited|theft|yield)
  (any|every) (user|caller|attacker)[^.]{0,140}(steal|stole|stolen|drain|drains|drained|extract|extracts|extracted|profit|profits)
  steals? (the )?(pending |unclaimed |accrued )?yield
```

## Known false-positive modes

These are the shapes where the rule fires on something it should not. They are the
reason a firing is a prompt to check, not a verdict.

- A finding that is atomic but describes the atomic path in a way the patterns do not phrase as one transaction.
- A private-mempool or builder scenario where front-running is not available to an outsider but the ordering bug is still real.
- A report where "front-run" appears in a mitigation note rather than in the attack path. That now holds instead of killing, and it is still a false hold.

## Synthetic examples

Both examples are synthetic. They describe no real report and no real target.

**Fires:** "The attack is front-run-only. The operator delay is the whole path."

**Does not fire:** "An unprivileged user steals the pending yield. A searcher can front-run the harvest."

## Corrective action

Find an atomic trigger path (flash loan, multicall, composed legos) or hold. A mention of front-running is not, by itself, a front-run-only finding. The front-run exclusion stops applying once the attack fits in one tx or an unprivileged caller extracts yield without winning a race.
